newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Pension Plan to widen investment portfolio.
newsitem.headline: Canada Pension Plan to widen investment portfolio.

text.p: The Canada Pension Plan (CPP) will no longer invest only in non-negotiable bonds under reforms proposed on Friday by Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin.
A statement from the federal Finance Department said new funds in the CPP would be "invested in a diversified portfolio of securities."
Provinces now borrow from the fund at federal rates but limited provincial borrowings would now be at their own market rates under the draft legislation he introduced.
Martin gave few details about how the new funds would be invested but said after a news conference: "They will invest in the same things the conventional pension funds invest in."

Asked at the news conference what rate of return a young person could expect, he said: "It is anticipated that the independently managed investment fund ought to have results comparable to private sector pension funds.
"I think that their assumption that they're using is about 3.8 percent in the fund, which is roughly what an actuary would use. But the actual rate of return will depend on government payouts."

An independent board appointed jointly by the federal and provincial governments would run the fund according to the same criteria as private funds under the Pension Benefits Standards Act, a Finance Department official told a briefing.
He said that for a transition period provision would be made for the provincial government borrowings.

"We'll allow a transitional rollover of those funds for the provinces. But thereafter after the transition period, the fund will largely be subject to the same sets of rules that a fund like the Teachers' Pension Fund would be applicable under the PBSA," he said.
With the Liberals' solid majority in the House of Commons, Parliament's elected chamber, there was little doubt of the passage of the proposed measures.
But the opposition Reform Party slammed the package.
"Today is a dark day for Canadians," Reform's Ian McClelland told a news conference, saying this amounted to one of the largest tax increases in Canadian history.
He said no Canadian would entrust his savings voluntarily to a government that was C$600 billion in debt and that was going to give a return far inferior to private mutual funds.
